newsitem.title: UK: Commodities-Metals try a rally, but copper falters late.
newsitem.headline: Commodities-Metals try a rally, but copper falters late.

text.p: World commodity markets generally ended the week little changed from Monday although industrial metals tried another rally and coffee was also firmer.
Traders said a weaker dollar and declines on bonds and equities on Thursday had sent some speculative money across to the commodity sector. Friday then saw something of a lull.
The flagship industrial metal, copper, which rebounded above $2,000 per tonne on Thursday, held most of the gains through Friday to close in London at $2,007.

But it eased just below $2,000 in later inter-office activity on one big sell order in thin volume that prompted some liquidation of long speculative positions. A burst of investment bank buying and shortcovering had pushed three months delivery London Metal Exchange (LME) copper higher towards the end of the week. Aluminium also firmed from a week ago on tight supply for January and speculative interest but ended Friday afternoon easing with copper to around $1,450.
Benchmark Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) wheat was little changed to a touch firmer from where it began the week, trading around $3.75 per bushel by the Friday mid-session.

Gold ended in London just easier at $378.95 per ounce but then firmed slightly on New York interest, and the benchmark Brent Blend of crude oil was steady to just firmer from Thursday around $22.65 per barrel.

Elsewhere in commodity markets coffee rallied after speculative buying in New York. Producer country selling has capped the advance but London January robusta type futures nonetheless ended Friday at $1,460 per tonne. This compared with $1,385 a week ago.
Cocoa held lower levels after a sell-off a week ago but sugar steadied from a sharp technical decline.
Freight rates extended a rebound from recent lows. The Baltic Freight Index (BFI) recorded its biggest single daily increase for more than 18 months, up 44 points to 1,477.

The index is compiled by the Baltic Exchange in London based on rates for key routes. Brokers said stronger-than-expected demand for grains and minerals in Asia had caused a 50 percent rise in chartering rates since September. Some key commodity prices at 1730 GMT on Friday
